modules.name: Arithmetic
modules.header:
Checked, wrapping and saturating integer arithmetic, at every integer width the language spells.
Each operation is generic over the integer type rather than repeated per width. Nothing here needs to be told which
type it has: an integer's zero, its all-ones pattern, its signedness and its two limits all follow from one operand
and the wrapping arithmetic the machine already does, so `int8` and `uint512` run the same code. Every helper below
derives what it needs the same way:
  zero     = value - value           the type's zero
  allOnes  = zero -% 1               every bit set: the maximum when unsigned, -1 when signed
  signed   = allOnes < zero          only a signed type reads all-ones as negative
  signBit  = 1 << (sizeof(T) * 8 - 1)  the top bit, which is the most negative value when signed
Ordinary `+`, `-` and `*` stop the program on overflow, so the checks below compute the wrapped answer with `+%`,
`-%` and `*%` and then ask whether it is the true one. The `Checked*` and `Saturating*` methods each integer type
carries are built on them, and they are the public spelling: the helpers below are this package's own, and
wrapping arithmetic is the operators `+%`, `-%` and `*%`.

modules.name: Atomic
modules.header:
Memory operations that other threads observe whole, and the orderings that say what they observe around them.
An ordinary load or store may be split, reordered or removed by the compiler and the processor, which is harmless
while one thread owns the memory and wrong the moment two share it. These intrinsics are compiled to the instructions
each architecture provides for shared memory: on x86-64 a plain `mov` for loads and weaker stores and `lock`-prefixed
instructions for the rest, and on AArch64 acquire and release forms with exclusive-access loops, so no part of an
atomic operation is ever seen half done.
They act on one value of 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits: an integer, a `bool` or a pointer. The ordering is always written at
the call, as a `MemoryOrder` case, so the compiler knows it while compiling; it says which other memory operations
may move across this one. `Rux/Atomic` wraps these in a type; they are here because only the compiler can emit them.

modules.name: Bits
modules.header:
Bit-level operations on integers, at every integer width the language spells.
Like the arithmetic beside them, these are written once and generic over the integer type rather than repeated per
width, and they derive what they need from one operand: `sizeof(T) * 8` is the width, `value - value` is the type's
zero, and `zero + 1` is its one.
Signedness is the thing to be careful about here, because `>>` is arithmetic on a signed type: it copies the sign
bit down instead of bringing zeros in. Every operation below that has to see a value's bits as bits rather than as
a number goes through `ShiftRightLogical`, which brings zeros in at either signedness. Reading a single bit with
`(value >> index) & 1` needs no such care — whatever arithmetic shift replicated above bit zero is masked away.
Nothing here is a machine instruction. A back end may recognize some of these shapes, but the count and reversal
operations are written as loops over the width so that a 512-bit type behaves exactly like an 8-bit one.

modules.name: Build
modules.header:
What the active build is doing, as ordinary values available while compiling.
`#build` answers questions about the build rather than about the machine it targets, which is `#target`'s job: the
profile chosen, what the profile implies, what artifact is coming out, and when it was made. Reading one costs
nothing at run time, because the value is folded where it is written.
The timestamp is fixed once per build rather than read per expression, so every use of it in one build agrees. That
makes it usable as a build identity and unusable as a clock.

modules.name: Cloneable
modules.header:
Cloneable: a type that can make an independent duplicate of a value it owns.
An owning type does not copy with `=`; duplicating one is an ordinary method call that may allocate, so the cost
is visible where it is paid. A `Clone` that allocates terminates the program when the allocation fails, as every
owning type does when it runs out of memory; a type whose callers may need to recover also offers
`TryClone() -> Self ! AllocError`, which is not part of this bound.

modules.name: Comparable
modules.header:
Ordering: which of two values of one type comes first.
One method, returning a three-way `Ordering` rather than a boolean, because two booleans cannot express
equality without being asked twice. A type that can be ordered can be sorted, searched and bounded by
everything in `Rux/Algorithms` without any of it knowing what the type is.

modules.name: Compiler
modules.header:
The compiler performing the build, and the version type it reports itself with.
`#compiler` is what a package uses to require a language feature rather than to guess at one from a version
number, which is what `HasFeature` is for. `SemanticVersion` lives here because the compiler's version is the
first thing that needed one; it is an ordinary value type usable for any version.

modules.name: Config
modules.header:
User-defined build values, read while compiling.
A project sets these in `[Build.Defines]` or on the command line with `--define`, which is how a build carries a
choice that is neither a target property nor a profile property — a feature switch, a vendor name, a limit.
Everything here is answered while compiling and produces no runtime code. A name that was never defined is absent
rather than empty, which `Has` is for: `Get` on an absent name yields an empty value that an intentionally empty
definition also yields.

modules.name: Convert
modules.header:
Conversions between primitive types that report what the cast alone does not: whether the value survived.
`as` always produces a value of the destination type, wrapping or truncating whatever did not fit and saying
nothing about it. That is the right default for the places a conversion is known to be safe, and the wrong one
everywhere else — an index narrowed to a smaller width, a signed count handed to an unsigned parameter, a
measurement rounded to a narrower float. These say what happened.
Every check here is a round trip: convert, convert back, and compare in the source type. Nothing compares a value
of one type against a value of another, so no comparison has to decide which of two widths or signednesses to use.
The round trip catches truncation on its own, and one further test catches the pairs it cannot see — a value and
its conversion that disagree in sign, which is how `-1` reaches `uint64` and how `2^63` reaches `int64` while
converting back to exactly what they started as.
A float source needs no special case. A NaN never equals itself, so the round trip reports it; an infinity converts
back to something finite; and a float narrowed past its precision comes back a different number.

modules.name: Copyable
modules.header:
Copyable: whether `=` may duplicate a value by copying its bytes.
The compiler knows this marker by name and decides it from the type's shape, so no extension implements it. A type
is copyable when it is plain data: it has no destructor, everything it holds is copyable, and it is not `#NoCopy`.
Every other type moves, and an owning type is duplicated by calling its `Clone` explicitly.

modules.name: Diagnostics
modules.header:
The four ways a program says something is wrong: two that stop it while it runs, and two that stop it being built.
`Assert` and `Panic` report and terminate. Neither unwinds, so no destructor runs on the way out — a program that
panics is not a program whose invariants still hold, and running cleanup code written on the assumption that they do
is how one failure becomes several. Anything that must be released on a failing path has to be released by a caller
that saw the failure, which is what a function returning `T ! E` is for.
`#Error` and `#Warn` produce no runtime code at all. They are evaluated where they are written, so a configuration
the package does not support is rejected while compiling rather than discovered by whoever runs the result.
All four take their message as a `char8[..]`, the type of an unprefixed string literal.

modules.name: Endian
modules.header:
Byte order: converting an integer between the target's own order and a named one, and moving it to and from bytes.
Two spellings of the same idea are published because they read differently at a call site. `ToLittleEndian` and its
three companions convert a value that is already in a register, which is what a caller writing a header field into
a struct wants. `StoreLittleEndian` and `LoadLittleEndian` move a value through raw bytes, which is what a caller
reading a file or a wire format wants, and they never require the bytes to be aligned for the value's type.
Every conversion asks `TargetIsLittleEndian` which order this machine has, rather than reading `#target.endian`.
The compile-time target is an intrinsic a package brings into scope by importing Core, which Core cannot do for
itself, so the order is established from the target's own storage instead — exactly, and by the one construct that
answers the question without being told: writing a value and reading back the byte it starts with.

modules.name: Equatable
modules.header:
Equality: whether two values of one type stand for the same thing.
Deliberately not derived from `Comparable`: a type can be equatable without being orderable, and forcing
an order on one that has none produces an arbitrary answer that later reads as meaningful.

modules.name: Floating
modules.header:
What a floating-point value is: a number, a zero with a sign, an infinity, or nothing at all.
Every predicate here is arithmetic. None reads the value's bits, which is what lets one implementation serve every
float width the language spells, including the ones lowered in software, whose storage carries padding no generic
function could locate a sign bit inside of. The identities they rest on are IEEE's own:
  value != value              only a NaN is unequal to itself
  value == value - value      only a zero is its own difference; a NaN and an infinity both give a NaN
  value == value + value      only a zero and an infinity double to themselves
  1 / value < 0               a zero's sign, which comparison cannot see, is the sign of the infinity it divides into
Not answered here: whether a finite value is normal or subnormal. Telling those apart needs the format's smallest
normal value, which is a per-width constant rather than something arithmetic recovers, so it belongs with the
per-width constants rather than in a function generic over all of them.

modules.name: Hashable
modules.header:
Hashing: the 64-bit summary a table uses to find a value quickly.
A hash is not an identity. Equal values must hash equally — a table is wrong otherwise — but unequal
values may collide, and a type that implements this must implement `Equatable` consistently with it.
The hasher is supplied by the caller rather than fixed here, so the same type can be hashed by a fast
non-cryptographic function in one table and by a keyed one in another; `Rux/Hash` provides both.

modules.name: Iteration
modules.header:
A cursor that yields a sequence of items one at a time.
The protocol `for` is written against. Nothing here owns a sequence or promises one can be traversed
twice: a cursor is consumed as it goes, and what happens if the sequence changes underneath it is the
sequence's business to document.

modules.name: Ordering
modules.header:
The answer a three-way comparison gives: which side is smaller, or that neither is.
Three cases rather than two booleans, so one comparison answers every question a caller can ask and a
type implementing `Comparable` is asked once rather than twice.

modules.name: Bool128
modules.header:
`bool128`: one of two values, stored in 128 bits.
Every boolean width holds exactly zero or one whatever its size, so a cast into one asks whether the whole source
value is non-zero rather than truncating to the width first.

modules.header:

modules.header:

modules.header:

Every boolean width holds exactly zero or one whatever its size, so a cast into one asks whether the whole source

modules.name: Bool8
modules.header:
`bool8`: one of two values, stored in 8 bits.
Every boolean width holds exactly zero or one whatever its size, so a cast into one asks whether the whole source
value is non-zero rather than truncating to the width first. This is the width `bool` names.

modules.name: Char128
modules.header:
`char128`: one Unicode scalar value, in sixteen bytes.
The same repertoire `char32` holds, in four times the storage: the range stops at U+10FFFF and the surrogates are
rejected, because a scalar value is what this carries. Its literals take the `c128` prefix; there is no `c128`
string encoding.

modules.name: Char16
modules.header:
`char16`: one UTF-16 code unit.
A code unit, not a character: every value that fits is valid, including a surrogate, which is exactly what a code
unit is. A scalar value outside the basic plane takes two of these.

modules.name: Char256
modules.header:
`char256`: one Unicode scalar value, in thirty-two bytes.
The same repertoire `char32` holds, in eight times the storage: the range stops at U+10FFFF and the surrogates are
rejected, because a scalar value is what this carries. Its literals take the `c256` prefix; there is no `c256`
string encoding.

modules.name: Char32
modules.header:
`char32`: one Unicode scalar value.
A scalar value rather than a code unit, so it stops at U+10FFFF and rejects the surrogate range whatever room the
width has beyond it. This is the width `char` names.

modules.name: Char512
modules.header:
`char512`: one Unicode scalar value, in sixty-four bytes.
The same repertoire `char32` holds, in sixteen times the storage: the range stops at U+10FFFF and the surrogates are
rejected, because a scalar value is what this carries. Its literals take the `c512` prefix; there is no `c512`
string encoding.

modules.name: Char64
modules.header:
`char64`: one Unicode scalar value, in eight bytes.
The same repertoire `char32` holds, in twice the storage: the range stops at U+10FFFF and the surrogates are
rejected, because a scalar value is what this carries. Its literals take the `c64` prefix; there is no `c64`
string encoding.

modules.name: Char8
modules.header:
`char8`: one UTF-8 code unit.
A code unit, not a character: every value that fits is valid, and a scalar value above U+007F takes more than one of
these. It does not widen implicitly to `char16` or `char32`, because a UTF-8 byte above 0x7F is not the unit of the
same number in either encoding.

modules.name: Float128
modules.header:
`float128`: IEEE 754 binary128.
One hundred and thirteen bits of significand, so about thirty-four decimal digits. Its arithmetic runs in software
on every target. The compiler supplies the finite limits, which are too long to be worth spelling out in decimal.

modules.name: Float16
modules.header:
`float16`: IEEE 754 binary16.
Eleven bits of significand, so about three decimal digits. Its arithmetic runs in software on every target.

modules.name: Float256
modules.header:
`float256`: IEEE 754 binary256.
Two hundred and thirty-seven bits of significand, so about seventy-one decimal digits. Its arithmetic runs in
software on every target. The compiler supplies the finite limits, which are too long to be worth spelling out in
decimal.

modules.name: Float32
modules.header:
`float32`: IEEE 754 binary32.
Twenty-four bits of significand, so about seven decimal digits round-trip. Rux/Format is what converts one to and
from decimal text exactly.

modules.name: Float512
modules.header:
`float512`: the binary512 interchange format.
Four hundred and eighty-nine bits of significand, so about one hundred and forty-seven decimal digits, following the
IEEE 754 progression of interchange widths. Its arithmetic runs in software on every target. The compiler supplies
the finite limits, which would run to hundreds of digits in decimal.

modules.name: Float64
modules.header:
`float64`: IEEE 754 binary64.
Fifty-three bits of significand, so about seventeen decimal digits round-trip. This is the width `float` names.

modules.name: Float8
modules.header:
`float8`: an eight-bit E4M3 float.
One sign bit, four exponent bits with a bias of seven and three fraction bits: four bits of significand, so about
one decimal digit. Unlike the E4M3 variant that trades them for range, it keeps IEEE 754's infinities and NaNs in
the all-ones exponent, which is why the largest finite value is 240 rather than 448. Its arithmetic runs in
software on every target.

modules.name: Float80
modules.header:
`float80`: x87 extended precision.
Sixty-four bits of significand with an explicit integer bit, so about nineteen decimal digits. The value is ten
bytes held in sixteen. On x86-64 its arithmetic runs on the x87 unit, and everywhere else in software. The compiler
supplies the finite limits, which are too long to be worth spelling out in decimal.

modules.name: Int
modules.header:
`int`: a signed integer the width of a pointer on the target.
Sixty-four bits on every currently supported target, and one of the two integer types whose width follows the target
rather than its name. A value that must keep its width across targets should name one that says it.

modules.name: Int128
modules.header:
`int128`: a signed integer in 128 bits, two's complement.
The range is asymmetric, as it is at every signed width: the most negative value has no positive counterpart, which
is behind nearly every edge case in checked arithmetic.

modules.name: Int16
modules.header:
`int16`: a signed integer in 16 bits, two's complement.
The range is asymmetric, as it is at every signed width: the most negative value has no positive counterpart, which
is behind nearly every edge case in checked arithmetic.

modules.name: Int256
modules.header:
`int256`: a signed integer in 256 bits, two's complement.
The range is asymmetric, as it is at every signed width: the most negative value has no positive counterpart, which
is behind nearly every edge case in checked arithmetic.

modules.name: Int32
modules.header:
`int32`: a signed integer in 32 bits, two's complement.
The range is asymmetric, as it is at every signed width: the most negative value has no positive counterpart, which
is behind nearly every edge case in checked arithmetic.

modules.name: Int512
modules.header:
`int512`: a signed integer in 512 bits, two's complement.
The range is asymmetric, as it is at every signed width: the most negative value has no positive counterpart, which
is behind nearly every edge case in checked arithmetic.

modules.name: Int64
modules.header:

The range is asymmetric, as it is at every signed width: the most negative value has no positive counterpart, which

modules.name: Int8
modules.header:

The range is asymmetric, as it is at every signed width: the most negative value has no positive counterpart, which
is behind nearly every edge case in checked arithmetic.

modules.name: Uint
modules.header:
`uint`: an unsigned integer the width of a pointer on the target.
Sixty-four bits on every currently supported target. This is the type a length, an index and a size are spelled in.

modules.name: Uint128
modules.header:
`uint128`: an unsigned integer in 128 bits.
Wrapping is defined at this width and `Min` is zero, so a subtraction that would go below it wraps rather than
trapping. Core's checked arithmetic is what reports instead of wrapping.

modules.name: Uint16
modules.header:
`uint16`: an unsigned integer in 16 bits.
Wrapping is defined at this width and `Min` is zero, so a subtraction that would go below it wraps rather than
trapping. Core's checked arithmetic is what reports instead of wrapping.

modules.name: Uint256
modules.header:
`uint256`: an unsigned integer in 256 bits.
Wrapping is defined at this width and `Min` is zero, so a subtraction that would go below it wraps rather than
trapping. Core's checked arithmetic is what reports instead of wrapping.

modules.name: Uint32
modules.header:

modules.header:

modules.header:

Wrapping is defined at this width and `Min` is zero, so a subtraction that would go below it wraps rather than

modules.name: Replace
modules.header:
Taking a value out of a place that keeps living: a field, an element, or the referent of a reference.
A plain assignment destroys the value it overwrites, and only a local, a parameter or a temporary can be given away
whole, so these two are the way to get the old value of any other place back: `Replace` installs a new value and
returns the one that was there, and `Swap` exchanges two places. Neither runs any code of the values it moves.

modules.name: Sendable
modules.header:
Sendable: whether a value may move to another thread.
The compiler knows this marker by name. A type is sendable unless it is or holds a reference, or a type declared
`#Unsendable`, such as a handle whose count is not atomic. A raw pointer is sendable: what it shares is the
program's to vouch for.

modules.name: Source
modules.header:
Where the reading expression is written, as ordinary values available while compiling.
`#source` is not one value: each field is filled in from the place it is read, so passing `#source.line` to a
function reports the caller's line rather than the function's, and so does a `#source` read written as a parameter's
default value. That is what makes it usable for a logging or assertion helper, which wants to name the site that
called it.

modules.name: Startup
modules.header:
Where a program's arguments and environment are when the kernel starts it.
An ELF kernel starts a program with its stack pointer at the argument count, followed by the argument pointers, a
null, the environment pointers, a null and the auxiliary vector. The entry stub keeps that address before it aligns
the stack and calls `Main`, and this is how a package reaches it. Windows and macOS hand a program its command line
through system calls instead, so there it is null.

modules.name: Target
modules.header:
The machine being compiled for, as ordinary values available while compiling.
`#target` answers questions about the target rather than about the host running the compiler, which is what makes a
cross-build produce the right code: a package selecting a syscall or a struct layout branches on these and never on
where it happens to be built.
Each variant names one system rather than a family, so the BSDs are told apart. A `when` on one of these keeps only
the branch that applies, so the untaken side is never resolved and may name declarations this target does not have.

modules.name: Zeroize
modules.header:
Clearing storage so that it stays cleared.
Erasing a secret is a write nothing reads back, which is exactly the write dead-store elimination is
entitled to delete, and ordinary source cannot say "and mean it". So this is a compiler intrinsic: the
guarantee is the compiler's rather than a library's, and there is no way to write it otherwise.
It clears the storage it is given and nothing else. A copy made earlier, a value the compiler spilled, or
bytes a reallocation left behind are all still there.

doc.summary: Which other memory operations may be reordered across an atomic one.
doc.markdown:
Which other memory operations may be reordered across an atomic one.
The weakest ordering that makes a program correct is also the fastest, and a stronger one is never wrong. When
in doubt, `SequentiallyConsistent` gives every thread one agreed order of all such operations.

cases.name: Relaxed
cases.doc:
No ordering: the operation itself is atomic, and nothing around it is held back. Right for counters whose
value no other memory depends on.

cases.name: Acquire
cases.doc:
Later operations of this thread are not moved before this load, so whatever a releasing thread wrote before
its release is visible after this acquire. For loads and the read half of read-modify-write operations.

cases.name: Release
cases.doc:
Earlier operations of this thread are not moved after this store, so they are visible to a thread that
acquires what it stores. For stores and the write half of read-modify-write operations.

cases.name: AcquireRelease
cases.doc: Both `Acquire` and `Release`, for a read-modify-write operation that does both.

cases.name: SequentiallyConsistent
cases.doc:
`AcquireRelease`, and also a single order of every sequentially consistent operation that all threads agree
on.

doc.summary: Reads the value at `address` atomically.
doc.markdown:
Reads the value at `address` atomically.
`order` must be `Relaxed`, `Acquire` or `SequentiallyConsistent`, written at the call. `address` must be aligned
to the size of `T` and point at memory every thread that touches it reaches only through atomic operations. Runs
in constant time and allocates nothing. Safety: `address` must point at a live `T`, aligned to its size, that
every thread reaches only through atomic operations while any of them may write it.

doc.summary: Writes `desired` to `address` if it holds `expected`, and returns what it held, as one atomic step.
doc.markdown:
Writes `desired` to `address` if it holds `expected`, and returns what it held, as one atomic step.
The write happened exactly when the returned value equals `expected`. `success` orders the operation when it
writes, and `failure` when it only reads; `failure` may not be `Release` or `AcquireRelease`, nor acquire more
than `success` does. `address` must be aligned to the size of `T`. Never fails spuriously. Runs in constant time
apart from contention and allocates nothing. Safety: `address` must point at a live `T`, aligned to its size,
that every thread reaches only through atomic operations while any of them may write it.

typeParams.name: T
typeParams.markdown: an integer of 8 to 64 bits, `bool`, or a pointer

params.name: address
params.markdown: the value to compare and replace

params.name: expected
params.markdown: the value `address` must hold for the write to happen

params.name: success
params.markdown: the ordering when the write happens

params.name: failure
params.markdown: the ordering when it does not

doc.returns: the value `address` held before the operation

A clone is independent of its source: each owns what it holds and releases it on its own, and changing one never

doc.summary: Ordering: which of two values of one type comes first.
doc.markdown:
Ordering: which of two values of one type comes first.
The bound a generic writes when it needs to sort, search a sorted sequence, or find an extreme. `Self` in the
signature is the implementing type, so a value is only ever ordered against another of its own type. An
implementation must be a total order: exactly one of less, equal or greater holds for any pair; reversing the
operands reverses the answer; and the relation is transitive, for the ordering and for the equality it reports.
A type with a value that compares unordered against everything, the way a floating-point NaN does, cannot
promise this and should not implement it. Algorithms that sort or search assume all three and may otherwise
loop, drop elements, or read past their bounds. A type implementing both this and `Equatable` must keep them
agreeable: `Compare` reports `Equal` exactly when `Equals` reports true.

Cannot fail: a total order places every pair.

items.signature: pub func ConvertChecked<From: Copyable, To: Copyable>(value: From, result: *var To) -> bool

doc.summary: Converts a primitive value to another primitive type and reports whether the true value was representable.
doc.markdown:
Converts a primitive value to another primitive type and reports whether the true value was representable.
`value` is read by value. `result` receives the conversion the machine produced, which is the true value when
this returns `false` and the wrapped, truncated or rounded one when it returns `true`; it is written in both
cases, so a caller who wants the lossy answer does not have to convert again. Returns `true` when the conversion
lost the value: a magnitude too large for the destination, a negative value converted to an unsigned type, a
value above the signed range converted to a signed type of the same width, a float with a fractional part
converted to an integer, or a float narrowed past its precision. A NaN and an infinity are both reported, since
neither survives a round trip. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing. Never traps, so the caller decides

doc.summary: Terminates the program unless `condition` holds.
doc.markdown:
Terminates the program unless `condition` holds.
`condition` and `message` are read by value; nothing is returned and nothing is taken ownership of. `message`
should say what was expected rather than what was found, since the value that failed is not printed. Reports the
message, the enclosing function, and the file, line and column of the call, then terminates. Does not unwind: no
destructor runs, and no caller observes the failure. Present in every build, so it is the right check for a
contract that must hold in a released program. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

doc.summary: Equality: whether two values of one type stand for the same thing.
doc.markdown:
Equality: whether two values of one type stand for the same thing.
The bound a generic writes when it needs to compare its element type — a search, a deduplication, a hash table's
key. `Self` in the signature is the implementing type, so an `Equatable` value is only ever compared against
another of its own type and never against an unrelated one. An implementation must be an equivalence: a value
equals itself, equality reads the same in either order, and two values each equal to a third are equal to each
other. A type that cannot promise all three — one with a value that does not equal itself, the way a
floating-point NaN does not — should not implement this, and callers relying on it are entitled to assume it
holds. A type that also implements `Hashable` must keep the two agreeable: equal values hash the same.

doc.summary: Reports whether this value and `other` are equal.
doc.markdown:
Reports whether this value and `other` are equal.
Borrows both operands and takes ownership of neither, so comparing costs nothing and leaves both usable.
The reference guarantees that `other` is present.
Cannot fail: every pair of values of the type is either equal or not.

doc.markdown:
Whether the value is the zero that carries a minus sign.
`value` is read by value. `-0.0` reports `true` and `+0.0` reports `false`, though the two compare equal; every
other value, NaN included, reports `false`.
The sign of a zero is invisible to comparison, so it is read from the infinity the zero divides into: `1 / -0.0`

dividing by zero is a defined floating-point operation rather than an error.

Whether the value carries a minus sign.

Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

Whether the value carries a plus sign.

doc.summary: Hashing: the 64-bit summary a table uses to find a value quickly.
doc.markdown:
Hashing: the 64-bit summary a table uses to find a value quickly.
The bound a generic writes when it keys a hash table or a set on its element type. The one rule an
implementation must keep is agreement with equality: two values that are equal must hash the same. The converse
is not required, and unequal values sharing a hash is an ordinary collision rather than a fault. Hashing the
same value twice in one program run must give the same answer, so an implementation must read only the value
itself — not an address, not a counter, not the clock. A hash is not a checksum and not a digest: it is not
stable across program runs, across compiler versions, or across targets, and nothing that outlives the process
should be keyed on one. `Rux/Hash` supplies the named, documented algorithms for that, and `Rux/Crypto` the ones
that must resist an adversary.

doc.summary: The hash of this value.
doc.markdown:
The hash of this value.
Borrows the value and takes ownership of nothing, so hashing leaves it usable.
Cannot fail. Every value of the type has a hash, and the same value always gives the same one within a run.
doc.returns: this value's hash

doc.summary: A cursor that yields a sequence of items one at a time.
doc.markdown:
A cursor that yields a sequence of items one at a time.
The compiler drives iteration by shape rather than through this interface: a `for` loop accepts any type with a
`func Next(&var self) -> Item?`, which advances the cursor and reports either the next item or, with `none`,
that the sequence has ended. The item type is whatever that optional carries, and it differs per iterator, so
the method is not written here; the generic `Cursor<T>` names it for bounds, which is how the adaptors take an
iterator. What this interface adds is the name. `extend MyCursor : Iterator` records that a type means to be an
iterator and documents which of its methods carry the protocol, and a bound written `<T: Iterator>` says what a
generic expects of its argument. Neither is required to iterate, and a bound on it grants no operations, so a
generic that needs to advance a cursor itself should take the concrete iterator type. An iterator is consumed as
it is read: `Next` mutates it, and an iterator that has reported `none` keeps reporting `none`. Nothing here
promises an iterator can be restarted or copied. An iterator borrows whatever it walks over. Modifying that
container while an iterator over it is alive — growing a vector, rehashing a map, freeing the storage — leaves
the iterator pointing at storage that has moved or gone, and reading it afterwards is undefined. Finish with the
iterator before touching the container.

doc.summary: A value that can hand out an `Iterator` over its contents.
doc.markdown:
A value that can hand out an `Iterator` over its contents.
As with `Iterator`, the compiler matches this by shape: a `for` loop accepts any type with a `func Iterate()`
that returns an iterator, and calls it once at the top of the loop. The returned type differs per container, so
the method cannot be written here either. `extend MyContainer : Iterable` records the intent and names the
protocol; iterating does not require it. Arrays, slices and ranges are iterated directly by the compiler and
implement nothing. The iterator handed out borrows the container, so the container must outlive it and must not
be modified while it is alive. See `Iterator`.

doc.summary: The answer a three-way comparison gives: which side is smaller, or that neither is.
doc.markdown:
The answer a three-way comparison gives: which side is smaller, or that neither is.
The discriminants are `-1`, `0` and `1` stored in an `int8`, so an ordering costs one byte and its sign is the
comparison's sign. A comparison that cannot decide has no representation here: every pair a comparison is asked
about must land on exactly one of these three.
`Ordering` is a `Copy` value, so reading one never consumes it.

items.name: Machine::Zeroize
items.signature: pub func Zeroize(memory: *var uint8, length: uint64)

doc.summary: Overwrites a byte range with zeros, and is never removed however unread those bytes are afterwards.
doc.markdown:
Overwrites a byte range with zeros, and is never removed however unread those bytes are afterwards.
Safety: `memory` is borrowed for the call and must address at least `length` writable bytes; passing fewer, or a
null pointer with a non-zero length, is undefined. `length` of zero writes nothing. Nothing is returned.
Clearing a secret is a write nothing reads back, which is exactly what dead-store elimination is entitled to
delete. Ordinary source cannot say "and mean it", so this is a compiler guarantee rather than a library one:
every write the call lowers to is marked as one that must happen. Runs in time proportional to `length` and
allocates nothing. It clears the storage it is given and nothing else — a value copied elsewhere beforehand, or
spilled to a register or the stack by the caller, is not reached.
